clinicalPearls: Relapsing fever is caused by several Borrelia spirochete species and occurs in three epidemiologic forms: louse-borne (LBRF, B. recurrentis), soft tick-borne (STRF, multiple Ornithodoros-transmitted species), and hard tick-borne (HTRF, mainly B. miyamotoi and B. lonestari) (p.1444).

The hallmark is two or more febrile episodes separated by afebrile intervals of well-being; the relapsing course reflects antigenic variation of the spirochete's surface lipoproteins, with each variant cleared as specific antibody develops (p.1444-1446).

In LBRF the first fever is typically unremitting for 3-6 days and is usually followed by a single milder relapse, whereas STRF produces multiple febrile periods of 1-3 days each; interfebrile intervals span roughly 4-14 days (p.1446).

A 'crisis' may terminate the first fever episode (rigors, a further rise in temperature, increased pulse and blood pressure for about 15-30 min), followed by drenching sweats, falling temperature, and hypotension lasting several hours (p.1446).
Soft ticks (Ornithodoros) feed briefly, often under 30 minutes and usually while the victim sleeps, then leave undetected, so the exposure may go unrecognized (p.1445).
Transovarial transmission in soft ticks means infection risk can persist in a dwelling for years, and a case may be diagnosed long after the last reported local case (p.1445-1447).

LBRF is acquired not from the louse bite itself but by rubbing crushed louse hemolymph into the bite site or auto-inoculating it into conjunctivae or a wound; humans are the sole reservoir of B. recurrentis (p.1445).
Jaundice, epistaxis, and subconjunctival hemorrhages are common in LBRF but typically absent in STRF and HTRF; splenomegaly or splenic tenderness is common in both LBRF and STRF (p.1446).

Localizing neurologic signs are more frequent in STRF than in LBRF/HTRF; B. turicatae is notably neurotropic, and unilateral or bilateral Bell's palsy (cranial neuritis) characteristically appears in the second or third febrile episode rather than the first (p.1446).

B. miyamotoi disease (HTRF) is less distinctive, often presenting as acute fever with chills, headache, and myalgia 1-2 weeks after a tick bite, and has been mistaken for undifferentiated sepsis; meningoencephalitis occurs particularly in patients with impaired humoral immunity (e.g., after rituximab) (p.1446).

Diagnosis of LBRF/STRF rests on direct microscopic detection of spirochetes in blood (Wright, Giemsa, or Giemsa-Wright stain), best collected at or just before the fever peak; spirochete density in B. miyamotoi/B. lonestari may be too low for smear alone (p.1447).

Outbreaks of LBRF (often alongside typhus) cluster in settings of famine, war, refugee migration, homelessness, and incarceration, and can appear in migrant camps far from the country of origin (p.1445).
harrison.pathophysiology: Borrelia are slender, double-membrane spirochetes that are extracellular pathogens with a limited biosynthetic genome about one-quarter the size of E. coli; their flagella lie between the two membranes. Tick-borne spirochetes enter in tick saliva at the onset of feeding, and from a small inoculum STRF organisms proliferate in blood (doubling roughly every 6 h) to 10^6-10^7/mL or more, while HTRF organisms grow more slowly to lower densities. Although they lack potent exotoxins and lack lipopolysaccharide endotoxin, abundant Borrelia lipoproteins activate Toll-like receptors, driving an endotoxemia-like proinflammatory response with elevated TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-8. Spirochete binding to erythrocytes causes red cell aggregation, splenic/hepatic sequestration, hepatosplenomegaly, and anemia; bleeding reflects thrombocytopenia, impaired hepatic clotting-factor production, and small-vessel blockage by aggregates of spirochetes, erythrocytes, and platelets. Serotype-specific IgM appears after a few days and lyses circulating bacteria by bactericidal action or opsonization; release of bacterial products from dying organisms drives a spontaneous 'crisis,' the antibiotic-triggered counterpart of which is the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. Antigenic variation of surface lipoproteins produces successive bacteremic relapses, each ended by variant-specific antibody. Some species are neurotropic and enter the relatively immune-sheltered brain, and spirochetes can cross the maternal-fetal barrier to cause placental damage, intrauterine growth retardation, and congenital infection (p.1444-1447).
additionalDifferentials: Rocky Mountain spotted fever and other rickettsioses
Tick-borne viral infection (including a viral encephalitis transmitted by Ixodes)
Lyme disease (especially when STRF presents with Bell's palsy in co-endemic areas)
Influenza (LBRF cough plus fever and myalgia can mimic it)
Undifferentiated sepsis (notably with B. miyamotoi disease)
infectionMimics: Malaria (periodic fever, co-endemic, can coexist as co-infection)
Epidemic louse-borne typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii) and other rickettsioses
Lyme disease (cross-reactive serology and shared Bell's palsy)
additionalInvestigations: Wright, Giemsa, or Giemsa-Wright-stained thin blood smear examined over several oil-immersion fields (sensitive when spirochete density is >= 10^5/mL), ideally drawn at or just before the fever peak
Thick blood smear treated with 0.5% acetic acid before staining, or a wet mount of citrated blood examined by phase-contrast/dark-field microscopy for motile spirochetes
PCR / nucleic acid amplification testing of blood or CSF (more sensitive than thin smear, especially between febrile episodes; preferred for B. miyamotoi and B. lonestari)
Culture of blood or CSF in Barbour-Stoenner-Kelly broth medium (slow, rarely offered)
GlpQ-based serologic assay (specific for relapsing-fever Borrelia and negative in Lyme disease species, but often negative when smear/PCR are positive)
CSF analysis in any case with signs of meningitis/meningoencephalitis (mononuclear pleocytosis and mildly-to-moderately elevated protein support CNS involvement)
Complete blood count (normocytic anemia; variable leukocyte count; thrombocytopenia, sometimes <50,000/uL)
Liver enzymes and coagulation studies (elevated aminotransferases; PT/PTT may be moderately prolonged)
ECG and chest radiography where myocarditis is suspected (prolonged QTc, cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema)
redFlags: Signs of meningitis or meningoencephalitis (warrants CSF analysis and consideration of CNS-directed therapy)
Cranial neuritis, especially uni- or bilateral Bell's palsy, or visual impairment from iridocyclitis/panophthalmitis (which may be permanent)
Myocarditis: gallop rhythm, prolonged QTc, cardiomegaly, and pulmonary edema
Diffuse bleeding, jaundice, and poor liver function
Pregnancy (high risk of abortion, stillbirth, or perinatal death)
Abrupt clinical worsening within 1-3 h of starting antibiotics (Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with hypotension and falling platelets), which can be fatal without monitoring
harrison.prognosis: Untreated mortality is approximately 10-70% for LBRF and 4-10% for STRF, depending heavily on coexisting conditions (e.g., malnutrition, other infection) and available medical support. With prompt antibiotic treatment, mortality falls to about 2-5% for LBRF and under 2% for STRF; no deaths from HTRF have been reported. Poor-prognosis features include concurrent malaria, typhus, or typhoid; pregnancy; stupor or coma at admission; diffuse bleeding; poor liver function; myocarditis; and bronchopneumonia. The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in LBRF carries roughly a 5% mortality without adequate monitoring and resuscitation. LBRF or STRF in pregnancy frequently causes abortion, stillbirth, or perinatal death, though congenital malformations have not been reported. Documented posttreatment sequelae and prolonged disability have not been established for any form, and partial immunity to reinfection appears to develop in residents of perennially high-risk areas (p.1448).
pitfalls: Whole-cell serologic assays (including ELISA and the C6 peptide ELISA for Lyme disease) can be falsely positive in relapsing fever due to antigenic cross-reactivity among spirochetes (p.1447).
Serology cannot distinguish among Borrelia species as the cause, and a positive IgG on a single specimen may reflect past infection rather than the current illness (p.1447).
Specific serologic assays (e.g., GlpQ-based) are commonly negative at the very time a blood smear or PCR would be positive (p.1447).
Spirochete density in B. miyamotoi or B. lonestari infection may be too low for diagnosis by blood smear alone, so PCR is preferred (p.1447).
Smears drawn during afebrile intervals may miss spirochetemia; sampling at/just before the fever peak (or using NAAT) improves yield (p.1447).
For B. miyamotoi HTRF, prompt removal of an embedded tick may not prevent infection because transmission occurs soon after feeding begins (p.1447).
STRF presenting with Bell's palsy can be misdiagnosed as Lyme disease in co-endemic regions (p.1447).
Co-infections (malaria, typhus, typhoid with relapsing fever; B. miyamotoi with Lyme disease) may obscure the diagnosis (p.1447).
A Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can be provoked even by antibiotics with suboptimal antiborrelial activity (e.g., ciprofloxacin) given for an unsuspected case (p.1448).
harrison.severityClassification: No formal numeric severity score is given. Clinically, severity is stratified by relapsing-fever type and complications: LBRF carries higher untreated mortality (about 10-70%) than STRF (about 4-10%), while HTRF/B. miyamotoi disease is mildest with no reported deaths. CNS involvement (confirmed or suspected meningitis/meningoencephalitis, supported by CSF mononuclear pleocytosis and elevated protein) marks severe disease warranting parenteral therapy. Features defining a severe/poor-prognosis course include concurrent malaria, typhus, or typhoid; pregnancy; stupor or coma at admission; diffuse bleeding; poor liver function; myocarditis; and bronchopneumonia (p.1446-1448).
